extracted.intended_audience: students, statesmen, and general readers interested in constitutional design and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical conditions for forming and maintaining federal (and unitary) governments, and for governing dependencies; includes criteria for when union, federation, or separation is advisable and how to structure federal organs and powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for amalgamation of nationalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever really tends to the admixture of nationalities, and the blending of their attributes and peculiarities in a common union, is a benefit to the human race...But, to render this admixture possible, there must be peculiar conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that successful amalgamation depends on combinations of circumstances: relative numbers, relative civilization, whether the superior is able to acquire ascendancy or is overcome, and whether the governing majority treats the minority with tolerable justice and without exclusive privileges. Examples and contrasts: Norway/Scotland/England analogies, Bas-Breton and Alsatian acceptance into France, and Irish resentment explained by atrocious governance; assimilation is encouraged by equal justice, equal consideration, and removal of special grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles when nationalities are nearly equal
rubrics_metrics.description: The cases in which the greatest practical obstacles exist to the blending of nationalities are when the nationalities which have been bound together are nearly equal in numbers and in the other elements of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When approximately equal, each cultivates distinct peculiarities, revives obsolete customs and languages, sees rival functionaries as tyrannical, and regards concessions to one as taken from others. If aspirations to free government arise before fusion, separation is often necessary; geographical separation and lack of convenience in being under same government strengthen case for breaking the connection (e.g., Italian provinces under foreign yoke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federation advisable: sufficient mutual sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The first is that there should be a sufficient amount of mutual sympathy among the populations. The federation binds them always to fight on the same side...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathy can be of race, language, religion, and especially similarity of political institutions. Cites Switzerland as an example where sympathy maintained the federal bond despite religious difference; in America, differences over slavery undermined sympathy and threatened union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federation advisable: members must need union for defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A second condition of the stability of a federal government is that the separate states be not so powerful as to be able to rely for protection against foreign encroachment on their individual strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If states can defend themselves, they may see little gain and will withhold cooperation when federal policy differs from their own, risking dissolution of the union. Union is especially valuable where small free states are hemmed in by powerful monarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federation advisable: absence of marked inequality among members
rubrics_metrics.description: A third condition...is that there be not a very marked inequality of strength among the several contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While gradations exist, no single state should be so powerful as to rival many combined, else it will dominate joint deliberations (or two powerful states will jointly dominate). Illustrative critique: the German Bund where Austria and Prussia overpower smaller members and the confederation fails to achieve unified purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective federation requires federal authority binding on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two different modes of organizing a federal union...the federal authorities may represent the governments solely...or they may have the power of enacting laws and issuing orders which are binding directly on individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the latter (federal laws directly binding individuals) is the only principle likely to produce an effective federal government. Confederation of governments alone is merely an alliance, subject to contingencies; historical examples: Swiss pre-1847 and the early American confederation under the Articles failed, whereas the U.S. Constitution-model succeeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear constitutional limits and an independent umpire (judiciary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the more perfect mode of federation...it is evidently necessary...that the power to decide between them in any case of dispute should not reside in either of the governments, or in any functionary subject to it, but in an umpire independent of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessitates a Supreme Court and subordinate courts; constitutional limits must be precisely defined; states, federal government, and officials must be suable for exceeding powers. Advantages: impartial adjudication, decisions issued in concrete cases after argument, and public confidence based on judges' independence. Caution: decisions can shock public confidence (example: the judgment declaring slavery lawful in the Territories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal tribunals as substitutes for war/diplomacy between member states
rubrics_metrics.description: The tribunals which act as umpires between the federal and the state governments naturally also decide all disputes between two states, or between a citizen of one state and the government of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because war and diplomacy are precluded within a federation, a judicial remedy must supply their place; the Supreme Court dispenses international law within the union and is an example of an international tribunal for civilized society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal powers should include matters necessary to full benefits of union
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers of a federal government naturally extend not only to peace and war...but to making any other arrangements which are, in the opinion of the states, necessary to their enjoyment of the full benefits of union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of necessary federal powers: free mutual commerce (no frontier duties/custom-houses), exclusive control of customs/trade regulations, coinage, weights and measures, and post-office administration. Notes debates about federal scope (e.g., roads and canals) depend on how closely people wish to draw the federal tie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of local vs federal financial responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: If the general Legislature could not be depended on for being guided by the members for each province in modifying the general system of taxation...the Constitution might provide that as many of the expenses of the government as could by any possibility be made local should be defrayed by local rates imposed by the provincial assemblies...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: local expenses raised by provincial assemblies, general expenses (army/navy) apportioned among provinces according to resources and collected en bloc, with local assemblies levying the assigned contribution by methods acceptable locally. Historical example: French pays d'etats practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral federal legislature to balance population and state interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should consist of two houses, and...one of them is constituted according to population...the other should represent not the citizens, but the state governments, and every state...should be represented...by the same number of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: prevents undue power of populous states, guarantees reserved rights of state governments by requiring majority of states as well as citizens, and incidentally raises qualifications in the upper house (U.S. Senate historically chosen by state legislatures and populated by eminent men).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federations tend to reduce petty states and defensive aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: When the conditions exist for the formation of efficient and durable federal unions, the multiplication of them is always a benefit to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: diminishes number of small states not equal to their defense, weakens temptation to aggressive policy, ends wars and restrictions on commerce among members, and provides military strength mainly for defense. Notes that federations are less capable of sustained offensive conquest; exceptions (e.g., U.S. war with Mexico) often arise from sectional motives rather than national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide complete union vs mere federation by territorial and institutional fit
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether a country which is determined to be united should form a complete or a merely federal union...is sometimes necessarily decided by the mere territorial magnitude of the united whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different parts require essentially different governance such that one legislature and administration cannot satisfy them all, a federal arrangement (or separate legislatures) may be preferable. Example: England and Scotland maintained different legal systems under one Parliament; Italy's size does not preclude unity. Cultural/political inclinations (mania for uniformity on the Continent) affect feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect local peculiarities by granting large spheres to local authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it is not deemed necessary to maintain permanently, in the different provinces, different systems of jurisprudence...it is always practicable to reconcile minor diversities with the maintenance of unity of government. All that is needful is to give a sufficiently large sphere of action to the local authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include local governors, provincial assemblies for local purposes, local taxation for local expenses and constitutional guarantees against forced assimilation except by voluntary act. Examples: differing tax preferences, and English tolerance of anomalies facilitating unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different regimes for dependencies: military posts vs settled outlying territories
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary to discuss the case of small posts...which are held only as naval or military positions. The military or naval object is in this case paramount...the inhabitants ought to be allowed all liberties and privileges compatible with that restriction...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For strategic posts (Gibraltar, Aden, Heligoland), admit municipal self-management and liberties compatible with military necessity, and compensate by admitting inhabitants to equal rights elsewhere in the empire. Distinguish these from larger colonies or dependencies capable of representative government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependencies of similar civilization should have fullest internal self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlying territories...composed of people of similar civilization to the ruling country, capable of, and ripe for, representative government...this country has at length realized...that her colonies of European race, equally with the parent country, possess the fullest measure of internal self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonies allowed to form representative constitutions, govern by their own legislatures and executives on democratic principles; reserved veto of crown/parliament exercised rarely and only on imperial questions. Notes inconsistency of past colonial meddling and praises reforms (e.g., Lord Durham). Points out inequality remains in foreign policy (colonies compelled to join in wars without prior consultation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral principle: justice binds communities as it does individuals (critique of domination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who think that justice is as binding on communities as it is on individuals...feel even this limited amount of constitutional subordination on the part of the colonies to be a violation of principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses proposals to redress principle: colonial representatives in the British Legislature, or limiting imperial/parliamentary powers to internal policy and creating another representative body for imperial concerns where dependencies would be represented equally. Frames colonial domination as unjust and offers institutional remedies.
